result.summary: The Chorus of Argive elders praise Zeus for Troy's fall, reflect on pride and the grief of war, and doubt the beacon news until a Herald arrives. The Herald announces Agamemnon's return, Clytaemestra declares her loyalty, and the Herald reports that a storm scattered the fleet and Menelaüs is missing.

scenes.title: The Chorus on Zeus and ruin
scenes.summary: The Chorus thank Zeus and Night for Troy's fall, condemn Paris's crime, and describe the grief of Argive homes mourning the dead. They fear public anger and divine vengeance.
scenes.stakes: The city fears the people's resentment and the vengeance of the gods on those who prosper in wrong.

scenes.title: Elders doubt the beacon
scenes.summary: The elders debate whether the beacon news is true, then see a Herald approaching.
scenes.stakes: They risk false hope if the beacon news proves untrue.

scenes.title: The Herald returns
scenes.summary: The Herald greets his homeland, praises Agamemnon's victory, and exchanges words with the Chorus about hardships at Troy.
scenes.stakes: The Herald is overjoyed to have escaped death; the Chorus conceal old fears.

scenes.title: Clytaemestra's declaration
scenes.summary: Clytaemestra says she trusted the beacons despite mockery and sends a message of her faithfulness to Agamemnon. The Chorus doubt her sincerity and ask about Menelaüs.
scenes.stakes: Her pose of fidelity conceals her true intent; her honour is in question.

scenes.title: The storm and Menelaüs
scenes.summary: The Herald tells how a storm destroyed much of the fleet and separated Menelaüs's ship, leaving his fate unknown.
scenes.stakes: Menelaüs and many Achaeans may have died at sea.

alias_notes.explanation: Another name for Paris, the Trojan prince.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable warning that excessive glory invites divine ruin.
Shows the danger of public anger against rulers.

analysis.text: The Chorus link pride and excess wealth to ruin, suggesting Agamemnon's triumph carries danger. Divine justice punishes wrongdoing.
Dismissals of women's judgment reflect Athenian attitudes, and Clytaemestra's speech is deeply ironic.

language_notes.text: The 'meshed snare' and 'enthralling net' picture Troy caught like a fish or bird; 'enthralling' means enslaving, and 'o'erleap' means leap over.
Alexander is another name for Paris, the Trojan prince who carried off Helen. Zeus is 'lord of host and guest' as protector of hospitality.
'Temptation' (Greek Ate) is a personified force of blind folly that leads men to ruin.
The touchstone was a stone used to test precious metal; base metal shows dark when rubbed against it.
'Dower' means the dowry a bride brings; Helen brings war instead. 'Undareable' is the translator's coinage for a deed none should dare.
Ares, god of war, is pictured as a gold-dealer weighing bodies on scales; the dead return as ashes in urns.
The Spirits of Vengeance are the Erinyes (Furies), who punish bloodshed and wrongdoing.
"Heralded by a beacon" means announced by the signal fire; the news of Troy's fall has spread through Argos.
"To despond if the story change" means to fall into despair if the news proves false after he has rejoiced.
"'Tis" is a contraction of "it is"; "ere yet" means before.
The woman's mind has "boundaries open to quick encroachment": it is easily invaded by belief, like a poorly fenced field.
"Anon" means soon; "beguiled" means deceived or led astray.
"Boughs of olive overshaded" means his head is shaded by olive branches, a sign of a messenger bringing good news.
"God avert the omen of the contrary" is a prayer that bad news, the opposite of joy, not be spoken.
"Made shipwreck" means came to ruin; the Herald says most of his hopes failed, and he had not expected to be buried in Argos.
Pytho is Delphi, Apollo's oracle. "Pytho's lord" is Apollo, whose "shafts" are arrows that bring plague and death.
Apollo favored the Trojans in the war. Scamander is the river of Troy, where he was hostile to the Greeks.
Hermes is the gods' herald and patron of heralds, so the Herald calls him his own patron.
The "mattock of Zeus" is a digging tool; Troy is imagined as a field uprooted by Zeus's own hand.
Meaning: neither Paris nor Troy can claim that their crime cost less than the suffering it brought.
A legal image: Paris is "cast" (defeated) in a lawsuit for theft and loses everything, including his father's house.
"Malady" here is sickness; the Chorus wryly calls homesick longing a pleasing illness.
Ida is the mountain near Troy. The Greeks suffered its snows in winter and windless summer heat.
"Erewhile" means "a short time ago"; "Ilium" is another name for Troy.
"In good sooth ’tis like a woman" means "truly, it is just like a woman"; the speakers mock women as credulous and emotional.
"Fanes" are temples; "wont" means custom. Women raised a ritual cry while the incense fire was quieted or fed.
"Never having broken seal" means she has never been unfaithful; the image is of an unopened sealed storeroom or letter.
"Dyeing bronze" is an impossible act: she claims to know scandal as little as one knows how to dye bronze.
"Speciously" means plausibly but falsely; the Chorus says her words only seem fair to those who cannot read their hidden meaning.
Archaic inverted syntax: it means he cannot pass off false news as good so that his loved ones would rejoice in it for long.
Archery image: the Chorus's question hit exactly the point, compressing a long story of suffering into one question.
The Sun, as the god who sees everything, is the only one who could know whether Menelaüs lives.
The Herald means a joyful day should not be spoiled by bad news; gods of joy and gods of ill are kept separate.
The 'two-handled scourge' is a double-edged image for war, which strikes with two arms; 'Avenging Spirits' are the Furies, honoured in grim hymns.
'Evil shepherd' is a metaphor for the storm scattering ships like a flock; the 'blasts from Thrace' are the north wind.
Zeus is named here, though the translation elsewhere uses 'Heaven'; his mercy toward the race gives the Herald hope for Menelaüs.

context_notes.text: Night is invoked because Troy fell during the night, and the Chorus has just heard the beacon-fire news of its capture.
Paris, a Trojan prince, was a guest of Menelaus, son of Atreus, and abducted Menelaus's wife Helen, causing the Trojan War.
The sons of Atreus are Agamemnon and Menelaus, leaders of the Greek expedition.
Clytemnestra has just announced that a chain of beacon fires has carried news of Troy's capture to Argos.
The Herald is returning from Troy with news of the Greek army and Agamemnon. Olive branches signalled a favourable message.
The Elder's curse targets anyone who prays with ill intent against the city, hinting at the political unease in Argos.
Agamemnon is the elder son of Atreus; his younger brother is Menelaus. Agamemnon led the Greek army against Troy.
Priam was king of Troy; his sons include Paris, who abducted Helen and caused the war.
Clytaemestra is Agamemnon's wife. She stayed in Argos and will soon prove deadly to him.
Clytaemestra is Agamemnon's wife and queen of Argos, ruling while he is at Troy. She secretly plans to kill him.
Menelaüs is Agamemnon's brother and husband of Helen, whose abduction caused the Trojan War. His fate after Troy is uncertain.
Menelaüs is king of Sparta, brother of Agamemnon and husband of Helen, whose abduction caused the Trojan War.
Fire (lightning) and sea were natural enemies, yet here they combine against the Greeks; the Argives are the Greeks.
The Aegean is the sea between Greece and Asia Minor, crossed by the returning fleet.

literary_notes.text: Troy's fall is imagined as a net cast over the city, making destiny a trap no one can escape.
The wrongdoer is likened to base metal exposed by a touchstone and to a child chasing a bird, showing his folly.
Dreams slipping through the husband's arms and flying off on the paths of sleep vividly convey his empty longing.
Ares appears as a merchant weighing lives for gold, bitterly showing war as profiteering that returns only ashes.
The image of lightning striking the highest peak states the moral that excessive greatness invites divine ruin, and foreshadows Agamemnon's fate.
The Elder's question voices the chorus's doubt and sets up the tension between hope and distrust in Clytemnestra's report.
The elders' remark on women's credulity subtly points at Clytemnestra, whose word they distrust, and shows their prejudice.
Dust is called the "consorting sister of the mire", making it a witness that vouches for the herald's overland approach.
The fear of the "contrary" hints that the homecoming may bring grief rather than pure joy.
The Herald addresses the soil of Argos as if it could hear, showing deep emotion at returning home.
Troy's destruction is shown as plowing up a field, with Zeus's mattock as the instrument of divine justice.
Troy is pictured as an animal under a heavy yoke, suggesting total subjection.
The Herald's readiness to die foreshadows Agamemnon's coming death at home, which the audience anticipates.
The sea "sank to sleep" on a noon-day couch, vividly conveying the dead calm and oppressive heat.
Her pledge of faithfulness is false: the audience knows she has taken Aegisthus as lover and plans murder, so every word is double-edged.
Calling herself a watch-dog loyal to her master and hostile to his foes casts her as a guardian, ironically hinting at her real hostility.
The Chorus shows its wariness and perceptiveness, suggesting Clytaemestra's speech is deceptive and marking her as cunning.
The Chorus is likened to a master bowman, praising the precision of its question.
Fire and sea are given the will to swear an alliance, making the storm seem a deliberate conspiracy against the Greeks.
The sea 'flowering' with corpses turns a grim sight into a haunting image of beauty and death.
Saviour Fortune sits aboard the ship like a guardian, suggesting divine protection of the Herald's vessel.
